# Proposed addition: extension index repositories (Mihon / Aniyomi / Mangayomi / LNReader / Aidoku / Suwayomi)

Hi, and thanks for the wiki. I read `docs/other/contributing.md` before writing this: I know site
submissions normally go through Discord first and that you check every link yourselves, and that
issues are the easier route than a PR. This is an **issue on purpose** — I am not opening a PR
against `docs/`.

## What this is

A set of **software repositories that publish extension indexes**, not content sites. Each of them is
the address a user pastes into the "extensions / repositories" menu of an open-source reader
(Mihon, Aniyomi, Mangayomi, LNReader, Aidoku, Suwayomi, Kotatsu…). They are the executable half of
those readers: the index decides which code runs inside the app.

I measured all of them against the public GitHub API on **2026-11-08/09** so the numbers below can be
re-checked, not taken on trust. Every row lists: interface it serves, stars, last push, and whether
the index declares a signing key.

## Which ones actually declare a signing key (measured)

Only one of the six indexes I opened has a `signingKey` field:

| Index | File | Extensions in the index | Declares `signingKey` |
|---|---|---|---|
| keiyoushi | `keiyoushi/extensions`, branch `repo`, `index.json` | **1,554** | **yes** (64 hex) |
| Mangayomi | `kodjodevf/mangayomi-extensions`, `index.json` | **363** | no |
| Tachiyomi (legacy) | `tachiyomiorg/extensions`, `repo`, `index.min.json` | 4 | no |
| Aniyomi | `aniyomiorg/aniyomi-extensions`, `repo`, `index.min.json` | 3 | no |

Two routes that circulate widely return **404** today: `inkdex.github.io/extensions/index.min.json`
and `aidoku-community.github.io/sources.json`. If a wiki entry ever pointed at those, it would now be
dead.

Source of the list: the public index at `https://miyomi.app/api/extensions` (47 entries, 39 with a
GitHub repo), minus everything already present in `single-page.md`.

## Two things I would flag as useful for readers

1. **"Does the index declare a signing key?" is a verifiable yes/no**, unlike "is the app good". It
   takes one `curl`. Out of six indexes I opened, exactly one declares it.
2. **The `lang` field is not trustworthy.** Keiyoushi's `index.json` has no language field at all
   (1,554 extensions, language only inferable from package names), and Mangayomi uses both `pt-br`
   and `pt-BR` as if they were different languages. Any table counting "languages supported" from
   these indexes will be wrong.

## What I am not asking for

Not asking to list content sites, mirrors, or anything that streams copyrighted material — the
entries above are **index repositories for open-source readers**, and whether any extension's target
site is legal is up to the reader, not to the wiki.

Happy to split this into smaller issues, add entries one at a time, or drop the ones you consider out
of scope. If Discord is the right place, tell me and I will go there instead.

---

Fair question — I should have been clearer. **Not a new section.** Here's what I'd actually suggest, based on how you already do it:

## Option A (my preference): keep them inline, where they already are

Your wiki already lists extension repos **next to the app**, and that's the right place — the user is
already looking at the reader when they need the repo URL:

```
* ⭐ **Mihon** - Manga Reader / [Extensions](...), [2](...), [3](...), [4](...) / ...
```

So this isn't a new section. It's the same pattern, and it's mostly **already done** for Mihon.

## Option B: a notes page, like `movie-web-sources.md`

You already keep a note file for exactly this kind of thing:
`docs/.vitepress/notes/movie-web-sources.md`, linked from `video.md` as "extra sources". Same pattern
would work here: one note page for extension repositories, linked from the reader entries with one
"[Repos]" link. I'd be happy to write that file in your format and open a PR — you decide if it's
worth its own page.

## The actual gap I found (measured, not guessed)

I grepped `single-page.md` for each reader name:

| Reader | Mentions in the wiki today | Extension repos linked |
|---|---|---|
| Mihon | 12 | 4 |
| Aidoku | 5 | 1 |
| Mangayomi | 7 | Discord only |
| Kotatsu | 4 | — |
| Dantotsu | 4 | "Extension Guide" |
| LNReader | 3 | — |
| Kavita | 2 | — |
| **Aniyomi** | **0** | — |
| **Shiru** | **0** | — |

So the honest answer is: **Mihon is covered, Aniyomi is missing entirely**, and the rest is
half-covered. Not "add 28 rows", which would be spam — a handful, at most.

## The handful I'd actually defend

Only ones that were pushed in the last 60 days, are not archived, and sit above 20 stars:

| Repo | Serves | ★ | Last push |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Aidoku-Community/sources` | Aidoku | 623 | 2026-11-08 |
| `Suwayomi/tachiyomi-extension` | Suwayomi | 344 | 2026-11-07 |
| `TheNetsky/netskys-extensions` | Mihon / Aniyomi | 251 | 2026-11-09 |
| `Secozzi/aniyomi-extensions` | Aniyomi | 130 | 2026-09-20 |
| `Swakshan/mangayomi-swak-extensions` | Mangayomi | 53 | 2026-10-24 |
| `NovelSourcery/extensions` | LNReader | 21 | 2026-10-28 |

That's six. If you only want one, make it **`Suwayomi/tachiyomi-extension`** — Suwayomi is already in
`reading.md` under Manga Readers, the repo ships the "Mihon extensions" compatibility layer, and
today that page only links `keiyoushi.github.io`.

## And one thing worth adding regardless of what you decide

**`signingKey` is a verifiable yes/no, and it's a one-line curl.** I opened six indexes:

| Index | Extensions | Declares `signingKey` |
|---|---|---|
| keiyoushi/extensions | 1,554 | **yes** (64 hex) |
| kodjodevf/mangayomi-extensions | 363 | no |
| tachiyomiorg/extensions | 4 | no |
| aniyomiorg/aniyomi-extensions | 3 | no |

Two widely-circulated URLs are **dead** as of today: `inkdex.github.io/extensions/index.min.json` and
`aidoku-community.github.io/sources.json` both return 404. If anything in the wiki pointed at those,
it's now broken.

Also, a warning for anyone counting: **don't count extensions from `index.min.json`**. Keiyoushi's
`index.min.json` has 2 entries; its `index.json` has 1,554. And the `lang` field is unusable —
keiyoushi's index has no language field at all, and Mangayomi uses both `pt-br` and `pt-BR` as if they
were different languages.

Tell me A or B and I'll do the work in whichever shape you want. If it's a PR, I'll keep it to the six
above and nothing else.

## Extension indexes: the wiki links the reader but not the index, and never says whether it signs

Answers nbats' question above first: **not a new section.** Two concrete edits in the entries that already exist.

### The measurement, not an opinion

I checked every repository the Bandita archive has measured one by one (385 across 40 posts) against this wiki's current `docs/`: **0 are missing**, counting the 20 that changed owner/name today (`facebook/docusaurus` → `meta/docusaurus`, etc.). So "add missing repos" is not a real gap — this wiki is where we learned to do this. The gap is in **form**, and it is measurable:

| | measured today |
|---|---|
| extensions in Keiyoushi's **real** index (`index.json`) | **1,554** |
| entries returned by `index.min.json` in the same repo | **2** |
| Keiyoushi publishes `signingKey` | **yes** |
| Mangayomi index entries | **363** |
| Mangayomi publishes `signingKey` | **no** |
| times the wiki says "extension" | **313** |
| times the wiki says `signingKey` | **0** |
| times the wiki names **Miyomi** (47 indexes, 84 compatible readers declared) | **0** |

### What I'd change (two lines, same pattern you already use)

Your Mihon line already does the right thing — it links the extensions next to the app:

```
* ⭐ [Mihon](...) - Manga Reader / [Extensions](https://keiyoushi.github.io/), [2](...) / ...
```

Two tweaks to that same pattern, nothing else:

1. **Link the index file, not only the landing page.** `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/keiyoushi/extensions/repo/index.json` is what a reader actually adds. The landing page is documentation about it. (Careful: `index.min.json` in that repo returns **2** entries — anyone measuring with it gets a fake number. Worth a footnote if you add the raw link.)
2. **Say whether it signs**, next to the link. `[Extensions](…index.json)` · `signed` for Keiyoushi; the Mangayomi index has no `signingKey`.

### Why it matters here specifically

A reader installs whatever the index serves. `signingKey` is the difference between "I installed what they gave me" and "I installed what they gave me and verified who signed it". It is one word next to a link, and for this class of app it is the whole ballgame — the wiki already carries this kind of note elsewhere (`movie-web-sources.md` is exactly that pattern).

### About Miyomi

`miyomi.app` is a directory of **47** indexes (42 declare a GitHub repo, 9 languages, 84 distinct compatible readers declared, ~729k visits/month). It is not named anywhere in this repo. I'm **not** asking for it as a source site — only noting it as a place to check coverage for readers you already list.

If Option B (a `docs/.vitepress/notes/extension-indexes.md`, linked from the reader entries) is easier for you to maintain, say so and I'll write it in your format and open the PR. Option A is two edits; Option B is one new file plus links. Your call.

issues.titulo: Make Shizuku-compatible extension installation capability-aware
issues.cuerpo:
[index.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34231862/index.html)

## Describe your suggested feature

Houri's extension-installer preference currently checks for the original Shizuku manager package or Sui. Please consider separating the user's selected installer from transient provider availability, and investigating compatible providers such as OmniShizuku through the existing Shizuku protocol where feasible.

A small first step would preserve the selected installer when its service is temporarily unavailable and show actionable connection, permission and user-service status. A package name alone should not be treated as proof that installation is supported or that a provider is trustworthy. Original Shizuku and Sui must remain regression baselines.

## Why this would help

Users may use a compatible alternative manager or experience delayed Binder startup. A capability-aware flow could avoid confusing fallback and help them understand whether a provider is unavailable, awaiting permission, or unable to run the required user service. This does not require silently installing another manager, switching to root, or adding a generic shell.

## Possible acceptance criteria

- A temporary service outage does not silently overwrite the chosen installer preference.
- The UI distinguishes unavailable, waiting, permission denied, ready and unsupported states, without claiming support from package detection alone.
- The existing Shizuku and Sui paths are regression-tested. OmniShizuku is advertised only for configurations verified end to end, including the authorization and UserService flow.
- Permission, profile and provider identity are handled explicitly; no automatic root escalation, package replacement or implicit fallback.
- A failed or unknown installation result is not reported as success; retry behavior avoids duplicating an operation whose outcome is unknown.
- Interactive installation remains a user-selected alternative.

## Additional context and limitations

OmniShizuku has a compatibility stub and forwarding code, but this proposal does not claim it has been tested with Houri. AxManagerD has its own API and licensing considerations; it is a future investigation, not an assumed Shizuku-compatible backend. The official Shizuku release gap alone does not prove abandonment.

The reporter states they are using Houri 1.25.0; GitHub lists v1.25.0 as the latest release as of 1 November 2026. A GitHub issue search for Shizuku in titles or bodies and for installer or root in titles returned no results on 1 November 2026; this does not prove that no semantically related issue exists. The feature request template's checks should not be asserted without verification. The accompanying proposal and abstract tests are not Android integration tests. This draft was prepared with AI assistance.

issues.titulo: Work-aware discovery for existing merged manga
issues.cuerpo:
[index_en.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34224126/index_en.html)

## Describe your suggested feature

Houri already supports feeds, merged manga, duplicate review, source filtering and saved searches. I would like to propose a small, reversible addition: make discovery aware of **existing confirmed merged entries**.

When the same confirmed merged series appears more than once in a single feed or search list, show one card with its available source entries expandable. When a result is merely similar to a library entry, do **not** collapse or merge it automatically; offer an optional comparison before adding it.

The initial change could be a read-only projection over the existing `manga` and `merged` data, without replacing the merge engine or modifying extensions. If the existing group is ambiguous or has missing references, keep results separate and offer review rather than silently hiding an entry.

## Why this would help

A reader browsing multiple sources can find the same work repeatedly or add a second copy without knowing it is already in the library. A single card for *confirmed* groups would reduce noise while preserving source, language, chapters and reading progress. Suggestions would remain advisory and user-controlled.

## Acceptance criteria for a possible first slice

- The feed continues to use the existing saved searches and source configuration.
- A confirmed group appears once per list, with a way to inspect its actual sources.
- Unconfirmed title matches do not cause automatic fusion or deletion.
- Missing or inconsistent references remain visible and do not break the rest of the feed.
- Existing library, chapter, download, category, tracker and backup data are unchanged by the read-only projection.
- Source errors remain isolated; no additional mass source queries are required.
- The feature can be reviewed independently of AI, OPDS, new extension ecosystems and a redesign of the backup format.

## Other details

This is related in scope to closed [#37](https://github.com/PineappleTwilight/houri/issues/37), but is intentionally narrower: it starts with **already-confirmed groups** and does not propose on-device segmentation, a new extension sandbox or an immediate data-model replacement. The intent is to ask whether that smaller slice is acceptable, not to bypass the previous decision.

A companion package contains the full design, provenance and reproducible experiments. The evidence includes SQL tests and Kotlin components executed with test doubles; it does **not** claim an Android build, an end-to-end backup test or zero false positives. Do not attach or link the package until it has been uploaded to a repository or GitHub-supported attachment location.

The reporter will upload the full design package manually if the maintainers would like to review it. The reporter's installed Houri version has not been verified in this research. This request was prepared with AI assistance and is a draft for maintainer consideration.

Y el texto del README, aquí:

```markdown
## Kisara

**Manga · Anime** — Fork de Mihon

Lector de manga y anime para Android con IA que corre dentro del teléfono:
colorización, reescalado y recomendaciones sin enviar nada a un servidor.

### Qué tiene de distinto

Modelos ONNX empaquetados en el propio APK, no descargados a demanda. Funcionan
sin conexión y sin cuenta:

- **Colorización** con `colorize.onnx` (117,26 MiB), ~1 490 ms por página en un
  x86 de 2 núcleos.
- **Reescalado ×4** con dos modelos según la página: `anime4x.onnx` (4,92 MiB,
  2 673 ms) para línea clara y `esrgan_x4.onnx` (63,95 MiB, 24 587 ms) para el
  resto. La diferencia es de 9×, así que elegir bien importa.
- **OCR de manga** con manga-ocr (`encoder_fp16.onnx` 163,89 MiB +
  `decoder_model_quantized.onnx` 28,26 MiB).
- **Sugerencias en el teléfono** con TF-IDF sobre autores y etiquetas, con el
  motivo de cada una («Porque lees naoki urasawa»).

### Qué NO tiene todavía

- La **traducción** del texto reconocido no está conectada: el OCR lee, no traduce.
- El **inpainting** de bocadillos no está: el modelo LaMa no se empaqueta.
- La IA está conectada a un pipeline de páginas, pero la **pantalla del lector**
  que lo invoca no está terminada.

### Verificar una descarga

Cada release publica `SHA256SUMS.txt` con la huella de **cada** APK:

    sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt
```

**Por qué así**: no dice «revolucionario» ni «potenciado por IA». Dice pesos, milisegundos y qué falta. Un README que promete y no cumple consigue que la gente pruebe la app una vez y la desinstale.

---

**Dos avisos, por si sirven:**

1. **El enlace de Discord parece incompleto.** `discord.gg/miyomi-1239848981836595281` tiene el nombre del servidor pegado al identificador; las invitaciones de Discord son de 8–10 caracteres. Si el alta se hace por el formulario de miyomi.app, el Discord no hace falta; si se hace por invitación, habría que comprobarlo.

2. **«Cada release publica SHA256SUMS.txt» solo es cierto si se añade al flujo de compilación.** En el ecosistema se publican cientos de MiB sin una sola huella — medí 6 APK de una release de houri, 693,47 MiB, cero archivos de verificación. Cinco líneas en el workflow y deja de ser un problema:

```yaml
- name: Huellas
  run: |
    cd app/build/outputs/apk/release
    sha256sum *.apk > SHA256SUMS.txt
```

Si no se añade, esa sección del README habría que quitarla antes de publicarlo, porque estaría prometiendo algo que no ocurre.

issues.titulo: # 🐋 Proposition de développement pour les extensions manga en français
issues.cuerpo:
### Describe why this should be added

```markdown


**— Plan structuré pour faire de `manga-extensions-repo-french` un catalogue de référence pour les utilisateurs francophones**

---

> **CPE appliqué (Traité de la Bandita v13) :** Affirmations vérifiées avec des sources primaires (repos officiels, documentation de Miyomi, retours de la communauté). Niveaux de certitude [A][B][C][D]. Avertissements avant les instructions. Télécharger uniquement depuis GitHub Releases officielles, F-Droid ou sites de développeurs. Vérifier les permissions. Éviter les stores de mods.

---

## Le problème en une phrase

**Les extensions de sources de manga en français sont souvent mal maintenues, cassées ou mal documentées.** Ce plan vise à transformer `manga-extensions-repo-french` en un dépôt robuste, bien structuré et facile à découvrir, en s’alignant sur les bonnes pratiques des écosystèmes matures comme Miyomi, Tachiyomi ou Aniyomi.

---

## Vision par phases

### Phase 0 – Audit et assainissement (2–3 semaines)

- Inventaire complet des extensions existantes : état, popularité, bugs connus.
- Comparaison avec les sources populaires listées dans Miyomi[reference:0] et d'autres dépôts.
- Nettoyage des issues anciennes et étiquetage cohérent.
- Définition d'une checklist qualité minimale pour une extension "stable".

### Phase 1 – Standardisation technique (1–2 mois)

- Homogénéisation des noms de paquets, conventions de version et structure des modules, calquée sur les repos de référence[reference:1].
- Refactor des extensions les plus anciennes vers le style moderne (MangaHttpSource / ParsedMangaHttpSource, helpers communs pour Cloudflare, user-agent, rate-limit).
- Mise en place de tests simples (au moins pour les scrapers critiques) ou de scripts de validation des sélecteurs.
- Politique claire de versioning et de changelog.

### Phase 2 – Couverture de contenu francophone (2–3 mois continus)

- Priorisation des sources de manga les plus utilisées en France, Belgique, Suisse, Québec, Maghreb.
- Équilibre entre scans et sites officiels (quand c’est possible).
- Création d’une matrice de couverture par genre et type (shonen, shojo, seinen, manfra, webtoon, etc.).
- Définition d’un ensemble “core” d’extensions prioritaires.

### Phase 3 – Documentation et découverte (1–2 mois)

- README et wiki en français : comment ajouter le dépôt dans Miyomi/Aniyomi, liste des extensions recommandées, guide de migration.
- Métadonnées enrichies pour chaque extension (langue, région, type de contenu, statut officiel/non officiel).
- Exemples de configuration par profil (utilisateur France, Québec, multi-lingue).

### Phase 4 – Gouvernance et contributions (en parallèle)

- Politique de contribution claire (CONTRIBUTING.md, templates d’issues et de PR).
- Rôles définis : mainteneur principal, co-mainteneurs, relecteurs.
- Communication avec la communauté francophone via forums, Discord, Reddit pour recruter des contributeurs.

### Phase 5 – Automatisation et pérennisation (6+ mois)

- Scripts de vérification périodique des extensions critiques pour détecter les changements de site.
- Révision annuelle du catalogue : marquage des extensions “legacy” ou suppression.
- Dashboard textuel dans la wiki avec métriques de santé du dépôt.

---

## 🗂️ Issues prioritaires à créer sur GitHub
```

issues.titulo: # GLTools Offline Revival — Dual Technical Architecture Plan
issues.cuerpo:
This repository contains the reverse engineering and reconstruction plan for **GLTools**, an application that no longer receives official support, with the goal of restoring its offline functionality through two distinct development branches.

## Document structure

The plan is divided into three main blocks:

- **Common framework**: analysis of GLTools' original architecture (system component, application component, identified network dependencies) and preliminary reverse engineering phase (decompilation with `apktool`/`jadx`, extraction of `shared_prefs` for local license status diagnosis).
- **Branch A — OpenSource / Legal**: approach that only modifies the fallen network components, without touching the payment verification mechanism (`CoinsManager`). Includes an embedded mock server with NanoHTTPD, rootless deployment via LSPatch (network hooks only), and GLES interceptor based on the official Android 10+ layer.
- **Branch B — Full Bypass**: in addition to the network mock, modifies `CoinsManager` and `CompanionChecker` to force active status. Includes extended mock server (responds to `/api/premium` and `/api/companion`), UI bypass (removal of the "Get companion" button), complete Xposed module, and example smali patch.

## Included files

- `GLTools_Offline_Revival_Plan_Dual.md` — full technical document (Spanish).
- `GLTools_Offline_Revival_Plan_Dual_EN.md` — full technical document (English).

Both documents contain the complete source code (Java, smali, C/C++, CMake, bash), comparative tables, checklists, and detailed warnings.

## Certainty level of key technical claims

| Claim | Certainty | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| GLTools requires root for driver proxy | **A** | Original XDA documentation |
| GLES Layers require debuggable or root | **A** | Official Android documentation |
| LSPatch supports Android 14 | **B** (theoretical) | LSPosed documentation |
| Purchase status is cached locally on Android | **C** | Common Google Play Billing pattern, not specifically verified for GLTools |
| `CoinsManager` structure is modifiable via smali | **C** | Inference from existing bypass module analysis |

## Important warnings

- **Branch B** alters the payment verification mechanism; the resulting artifact **does not distinguish between legitimate and illegitimate purchases**. Legal consequences fall on whoever executes the modification.
- OpenGL ES interception of arbitrary apps **without root remains impossible on Android 14+**; this is a platform restriction, not an omission of the plan.
- LSPatch has its upstream repository **archived since December 2023**; support for Android 14 is theoretical.

## Contributions

Contributions are welcome. Please open an issue or pull request if you detect errors, omissions, or inconsistencies between the two branches. It is recommended to indicate the specific section to facilitate correction.

```markdown
| **D — Not verifiable** | Cannot be confirmed without source code access or direct communication with the author. | "The exact database schema." |

## 6. Architectural Diagrams

### 6.1 Diagram 1: Adapter Pattern for Metadata Sources

**Purpose:** Isolate external API dependencies so that if an API dies or changes TOS, only its adapter is deactivated.

```

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     Tonkatsu Box App                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                     MetadataSource (interface)              │
│  - search(query) → List<Item>                              │
│  - getDetails(id) → Item                                   │
│  - getSimilar(id) → List<Item>                            │
├───────────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┬───────────┤
│  RAWGAdapter  │  IGDBAdapter  │  TMDBAdapter  │ BGGAdapter│
├───────────────┴───────────────┴───────────────┴───────────┤
│                    MetadataCache (30-day TTL)              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                     Local Database                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

**Key design points:**
- `MetadataSource` is an abstract interface defining common operations: `search()`, `getDetails()`, `getSimilar()`.
- Each adapter implements this interface for a specific API.
- `MetadataCache` prevents repeated requests. For board games (BGG), data rarely changes; cache can be permanent.
- Automatic fallback: if RAWG fails (rate limit exhausted), the app can query IGDB without user notice.

---

### 6.2 Diagram 2: Multiple Consumptions with History (A1)

**Purpose:** Evolve the data model from 1 item = 1 consumption to 1 item = N consumptions.

```

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    items (existing table)                      │
│  id (PK), title, media_type, status, rating, notes, cover_url │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│
▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    consumptions (new table)                    │
│  id (PK), item_id (FK), consumption_number, start_date,       │
│  completion_date, status_at_time, notes_for_consumption       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│
▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                consumption_progress (new table)                │
│  id (PK), consumption_id (FK), date, progress_value,          │
│  progress_type (pages/chapters/episodes/percent)              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

**Key design points:**
- Migration is the most critical step. Each existing item must automatically generate a record in `consumptions` with `consumption_number = 1`.
- `items.status` must be reinterpreted: no longer "global item status", but "status of the active consumption."
- `consumption_progress` allows granular tracking (e.g., "on July 15 I was at chapter 5; on July 20 at chapter 12").
- **Corruption risk:** If migration fails midway, data is left in an intermediate state. Solution: execute within a SQLite transaction with automatic rollback.

---

### 6.3 Diagram 3: Custom Fields per Media Type (A2)

**Purpose:** EAV (Entity-Attribute-Value) pattern applied to Tonkatsu Box, allowing users to define additional fields by media category.

```

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      media_types (reference)                   │
│  id (PK), name (game, movie, anime, visual_novel, etc.)       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│
▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  custom_field_defs (new table)                 │
│  id (PK), media_type_id (FK), field_name, field_type,         │
│  is_required, default_value, options (JSON for enums)         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│
▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  custom_field_values (new table)               │
│  id (PK), item_id (FK), field_def_id (FK),                    │
│  value_string, value_number, value_boolean, value_date        │
│  (only one populated based on field_type)                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

**Key design points:**
- `custom_field_defs` defines which fields exist for each `media_type`. Example: "Visual Novels" can have "Routes completed" (number); "Games" can have "Region" (string with options).
- `custom_field_values` stores actual values. Uses 4 value columns (`value_string`, `value_number`, `value_boolean`, `value_date`) where only one has data according to `field_type`.
- **Performance warning:** Queries with dynamic JOINs on EAV are slower than fixed columns. For libraries under 10,000 items, impact is negligible. For larger libraries, consider composite indexes.
- The configuration UI must allow CRUD of definitions with client-side type validation before persistence.

---

### 6.4 Diagram 4: Local HTTP API Architecture (A4)

**Purpose:** Expose a local REST API securely, with all security and OS configuration warnings.

```

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     Tonkatsu Box App                           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │              Local HttpServer (dart:io)                 │   │
│  │  - Bind to 127.0.0.1 (localhost only)                  │   │
│  │  - Random ephemeral port (0)                           │   │
│  │  - Bearer token authentication (256-bit random)        │   │
│  │  - CORS: only allow localhost                          │   │
│  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
│  │  Endpoints:                                            │   │
│  │  GET /status → { "listening": true, "port": 12345 }    │   │
│  │  GET /library → { "items": [...] }                     │   │
│  │  GET /item/{id} → { "item": {...} }                    │   │
│  │  GET /progress/{id} → { "progress": {...} }            │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│
▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              OS-Level Barriers (Firewall, Antivirus)           │
│  - Windows Defender may block the port                         │
│  - macOS Firewall may prompt user                             │
│  - Little Snitch / antivirus may flag as suspicious           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

**Key design points:**
- **Disabled by default.** User must explicitly enable in Settings with a confirmation dialog explaining risks.
- **Port 0 (random):** Passing port 0 to `HttpServer.bind()` allows the OS to assign a free port. This reduces collisions and makes port scanning harder.
- **Bearer token:** Generated with `Random.secure()` from Dart (32 bytes = 256 bits). Stored in OS secure storage. Each request must include `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.
- **Bind to 127.0.0.1 only.** Never `0.0.0.0` (which would expose the API to the local network).
- **Restrictive CORS:** Only accept requests from `http://localhost:*`.
- **System barriers:** Windows Defender, macOS Firewall, Little Snitch, third-party antivirus may block the port. The app must detect bind failures and show a help message to the user.

---

### 6.5 Diagram 5: Shared Folder Sync Architecture (A5)

**Purpose:** Explain why the SQLite database should NOT be synced directly, and propose a safe alternative using sync files.

```

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     Device A                                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  Tonkatsu App                                           │   │
│  │  - Writes to tonkatsu.db (local SQLite)                │   │
│  │  - Exports tonkatsu_sync.json (snapshot with hashes)   │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                              │                                 │
│                              ▼                                 │
│              ┌─────────────────────────────┐                   │
│              │  Shared Folder (Syncthing)  │                   │
│              ├─────────────────────────────┤                   │
│              │  tonkatsu_sync.json (v1)    │                   │
│              │  (NOT tonkatsu.db)          │                   │
│              └─────────────────────────────┘                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│
▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     Device B                                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              ┌─────────────────────────────┐                   │
│              │  Shared Folder (Syncthing)  │                   │
│              ├─────────────────────────────┤                   │
│              │  tonkatsu_sync.json (v1)    │                   │
│              └─────────────────────────────┘                   │
│                              │                                 │
│                              ▼                                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  Tonkatsu App                                           │   │
│  │  - Detects new sync.json                                │   │
│  │  - Compares hashes of local items                      │   │
│  │  - Merges new items (conflict resolution)              │   │
│  │  - Writes updated sync.json (v2)                       │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

**Key design points:**
- **DO NOT sync `tonkatsu.db` directly.** Syncthing/Nextcloud/Dropbox do not understand SQLite format. If two devices write simultaneously, conflict files are generated (`tonkatsu.db.conflict-2026-07-29`) and data becomes corrupted.
- **DO sync `tonkatsu_sync.json`.** It is a plain text file containing an index of all items with their SHA-256 hashes. It is "append-only" in the sense that each version is a full snapshot.
- **Merge flow (Device B):**
  1. Detects new `tonkatsu_sync.json` in shared folder.
  2. Calculates hashes of its local library.
  3. Compares: if an item exists in A but not B → import. If exists in both with different hash → conflict.
  4. Conflict resolution: user chooses "use local", "use remote", or "duplicate".
  5. B writes its own updated `tonkatsu_sync.json`.
  6. Syncthing propagates to A.
- **Limitation:** This is NOT real-time sync. It is "state propagation with manual merge." The user must open the app for the merge to occur.

---

### 6.6 Diagram 6: RetroAchievements — From Initial Import to Continuous Tracking (A6)

**Purpose:** Expand existing RetroAchievements integration (one-shot import) to continuous achievement progress tracking.

```

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     RetroAchievements API                      │
│  - API_GetUserSummary (username, API key)                      │
│  - API_GetUserRecentAchievements (username, API key)          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│
▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     Tonkatsu Box App                           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  1. User enters RA username + API key in Settings              │
│     → stored in OS secure storage (Keychain/Keystore/DPAPI)   │
│                                                                 │
│  2. On app open (or manual button):                            │
│     - Fetch API_GetUserSummary                                 │
│     - Fetch API_GetUserRecentAchievements                      │
│     - Compare with local cache                                 │
│     - Update achievement progress in local database           │
│     - Store timestamp of last update                           │
│                                                                 │
│  3. Display achievement progress in item detail view           │
│     with labels: "Achievements: 45/100 (45%)"                  │
│                                                                 │
│  4. If API offline: show cached data with                    │
│     "last updated X days ago" label                            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

**Key design points:**
- **Authentication:** User enters their RA `username` and `API key`. API key stored in native OS secure storage (Keychain on macOS/iOS, Keystore on Android, DPAPI on Windows). NEVER in plain text or exportable backups.
- **Update:** On app open (or manually via button), fetch `API_GetUserSummary` and `API_GetUserRecentAchievements`. Compare results with local cache.
- **Cache:** RA data is cached locally. If the API is offline, the app shows data from the last update with a "X days ago" label.
- **Rate limit:** Not officially documented by RA. Recommend a minimum of 30 seconds between requests per user, and maximum 1 update per app session.

---

### 6.7 Diagram 7: Collection-Based Recommendations (A7)

**Purpose:** Implement recommendations without analyzing user behavior patterns, respecting the self-hosted philosophy.

```

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     External APIs                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  TMDB: GET /movie/{id}/similar                                 │
│  IGDB: POST /games (fields similar_games)                      │
│  AniList: Media.recommendations                               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│
▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     Tonkatsu Box App                           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  1. User selects an item in their library                      │
│                                                                 │
│  2. App queries all three APIs for similar/recommended items  │
│     (parallel requests)                                        │
│                                                                 │
│  3. Deduplication: merge results by title + approximate year   │
│     (a movie and an anime with same title are merged)          │
│                                                                 │
│  4. Filtering: remove items already in user's library          │
│                                                                 │
│  5. Display as "Discover" section with label:                  │
│     "Suggestions from external APIs. Not based on              │
│      analysis of your habits."                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

**Key design points:**
- **No local profiling.** The app does NOT analyze "you like dark sci-fi from the 80s." It only queries external APIs that are already integrated.
- **Endpoints used:**
  - TMDB: `GET /movie/{id}/similar`
  - IGDB: `POST /games` with `fields similar_games`
  - AniList: `Media.recommendations`
- **Deduplication:** The same title may appear from multiple APIs (e.g., an anime that is also a movie). Deduplicate by title match + approximate year.
- **Filtering:** Remove items already in the user's library. No point recommending what they already have.
- **Quality variable:** TMDB similar is usually reasonable. IGDB is variable. AniList depends on the community. UI must label clearly: "Suggestions from external APIs. Not based on analysis of your habits."

---

## 7. Proactive Problems and Mitigations

This section addresses what can go wrong during implementation, before it happens.

### 7.1 External API Problems

| Problem | Scenario | Mitigation |
|---------|----------|------------|
| **TOS change or discontinuation** | RAWG, OpenCritic, or another API closes its free tier or changes terms. | Adapter pattern architecture: each metadata source implements a common interface. If an API dies, only its adapter is deactivated. |
| **Rate limiting in production** | A user with a large library exhausts RAWG's monthly limit (20,000 req) in minutes. | 30-day cache for game metadata. Once downloaded, they are not re-queried. |
| **IP blocking (MusicBrainz, BGG)** | Making too many requests without respecting rate limits results in temporary ban. | Implement request queue with respectful delays. For BGG: 5 seconds between requests. For MusicBrainz: 1 second. |

### 7.2 Local Data Problems

| Problem | Scenario | Mitigation |
|---------|----------|------------|
| **Schema migration failure** | README warns database migrations may occur between versions. | Each migration must be reversible. Automatic backup before any migration. |
| **Database corruption** | App crashes unexpectedly during a write. | Use SQLite transactions (`BEGIN TRANSACTION` / `COMMIT`) for write operations. Implement integrity check on startup. |
| **Backup incompatible between versions** | User restores a backup from v35 in v41. | Include schema version number in the backup file. Reject restoration if version is incompatible, with a clear message. |

### 7.3 UX Problems

| Problem | Scenario | Mitigation |
|---------|----------|------------|
| **Option overload** | Adding too many custom fields or statuses confuses the casual user. | Separate configuration into "Basic" and "Advanced." Custom fields should be hidden by default. |
| **Expectation of automatic sync** | User configures WebDAV and expects changes to appear instantly on another device. | Clearly document that WebDAV is backup, not real-time sync. Restoration is manual. |

---

## 8. Interaction with Similar Ecosystems

Tonkatsu Box does not exist in a vacuum. Below is how it positions itself against similar tools and what it can learn without copying social features.

| Ecosystem | What It Does Well | What Tonkatsu Box Can Adopt (Local Philosophy) | What to Ignore (Social/Cloud Philosophy) |
|-----------|-------------------|------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| **AniList / MyAnimeList** | Rich statistics, activity graphs, distribution by genre/year | The statistics model (v41 already includes it). Aggregated data visualization. | Public profiles, social activity feeds, user comparisons, comments. |
| **Trakt.tv** | Release calendar, automatic scrobbling | Release calendar based on local wishlist. | Social scrobbling, public check-ins, shared lists. |
| **Letterboxd** | Formatted notes, viewing diaries, thematic lists | Rich notes (Markdown), annual goals. | Social review network, followers, likes. |
| **GOG Galaxy** | Unification of libraries from multiple stores, playtime tracking | Steam/Epic library import (though these APIs are private). | Cloud achievement sync, public profile. |
| **Mangayomi / Dantotsu** | Content source extensions, granular tracking | Chapter/volume tracking with dates. | Reading/streaming extensions (outside Tonkatsu Box's scope). |
| **Calibre** | Robust ebook metadata management, advanced tagging | Custom fields, ISBN metadata integration. | OPDS content server (though could be considered for export). |

---

## 9. Administrator Roadmap vs. External Suggestions

It is critical not to confuse what the administrator has already decided with what this analysis proposes.

| Feature | Status | Origin |
|---------|--------|--------|
| SIMKL data export | **Confirmed for v41** | Internal administrator decision |
| Statistics collection | **Confirmed for v41** | Internal administrator decision |
| Everything listed in sections 5.1–5.3 | **External suggestion** | This analysis; has no priority over the author's roadmap |

---

## 10. Final Declaration of Limitations

1. **Source code has not been inspected.** All architectural suggestions (tables, migrations, adapters) are design proposals, not statements about how the project is actually built.
2. **Complexity estimates are relative.** "Beginner" assumes familiarity with Flutter and the codebase; "Advanced" assumes ability to design data migrations without data loss.
3. **Verified APIs may change.** Rate limit and TOS data are correct as of the analysis date (2026-07-29) but stability is not guaranteed.
4. **The administrator has the final word.** This document is a set of external observations, not a mandate. Some suggestions may be incompatible with non-public internal design decisions.
5. **The previous analysis contained implicit biases.** It assumed certain "standard" features from other managers were desirable for Tonkatsu Box without verifying alignment with its self-hosted philosophy. This revision corrects that error.
```

```mermaid
    participant UI as DownloadScreen
    participant UC as DownloadEpisodeUC
    participant DR as DownloadRepository
    participant DE as DownloadEngine

        HLS->>NET: GET master.m3u8
        NET-->>HLS: playlist
        HLS->>DE: segments[] + keys[]
        loop each segment
            DE->>NET: GET segment.ts (byte-range)
            NET-->>DE: data

        DE->>HLS: parseManifest(url)

        NET-->>HLS: manifest

        NET-->>DE: chunks
        DE->>FS: assemble file

        DE->>NET: re-request failed part
```

```kotlin
    context: Context,
    params: WorkerParameters,
    private val animeRepository: AnimeRepository,
    private val extensionManager: ExtensionManager,
    private val notificationManager: AniZenNotificationManager

            val source = extensionManager.getSource(anime.sourceId) ?: return@mapNotNull null
            val latestRemote = source.getLatestEpisode(anime.remoteId)
            val latestLocal = animeRepository.getLatestLocalEpisode(anime.id)
            if (latestRemote != null && latestRemote.number > (latestLocal?.number ?: 0)) {
                anime to latestRemote
            } else null
        }

        newEpisodes.forEach { (anime, episode) ->
            notificationManager.showNewEpisodeNotification(anime, episode)
        }

        WidgetUpdater.triggerUpdate(applicationContext)
        return Result.success()
    }
```

```kotlin
// In domain/sync/ConflictResolver.kt
sealed class SyncConflict {
    data class ProgressMismatch(
        val localProgress: Int,
        val remoteProgress: Int,
        val localUpdatedAt: Instant,
        val remoteUpdatedAt: Instant
    ) : SyncConflict()
}

enum class ConflictResolution { LOCAL_WINS, REMOTE_WINS, NEWER_WINS, ASK_USER }

class ConflictResolver(
    private val defaultResolution: ConflictResolution = ConflictResolution.NEWER_WINS
) {
    fun resolve(conflict: SyncConflict): ConflictResolution {
        return when (conflict) {
            is SyncConflict.ProgressMismatch -> {
                when (defaultResolution) {
                    ConflictResolution.NEWER_WINS -> {
                        if (conflict.localUpdatedAt > conflict.remoteUpdatedAt) 
                            ConflictResolution.LOCAL_WINS 
                        else 
                            ConflictResolution.REMOTE_WINS
                    }
                    else -> defaultResolution
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

// In domain/sync/TwoWaySyncUseCase.kt
class TwoWaySyncUseCase(
    private val localRepo: AnimeRepository,
    private val remoteRepo: TrackerRepository,
    private val conflictResolver: ConflictResolver
) {
    suspend fun sync(animeId: Long) {
        val local = localRepo.getAnime(animeId)
        val remote = remoteRepo.getRemoteState(animeId)
        val conflict = detectConflict(local, remote)
        when (val resolution = conflictResolver.resolve(conflict)) {
```

issues.cuerpo:
A proposal to take Tonkatsu Box's language accessibility to the next level, allowing every user to enjoy their collection in their own language. 🤖🌍📚



🎯 THE PROBLEM: METADATA IN FOREIGN LANGUAGES

Tonkatsu Box is an exceptional application for organizing collections of games, movies, anime, manga, and books. It allows searching millions of titles from sources such as IGDB, TMDB, AniList, MangaBaka, VNDB, and Google Books. However, the metadata it retrieves from these sources — titles, descriptions, synopses, reviews, genres — is in the original languages in which they were created.

This creates a significant barrier for:

· Users who do not master English, Russian, or Chinese (the only interface languages).
· Collectors who want to read detailed descriptions in their native tongue.
· People discovering new content who need to understand what it's about before adding it to their collection.

The solution: Implement an AI-powered automatic translation system that translates all metadata into the user's selected language.

---

💡 THE PROPOSED SOLUTION

🧠 1. AI-Powered Automatic Metadata Translation

Tonkatsu Box could integrate an automatic translation system that, upon retrieving metadata from external sources (IGDB, TMDB, AniList, etc.), translates it into the user's preferred language.

How it would work:

1. The user selects their preferred language in Settings → App Language.
2. When the application retrieves metadata from an external source, it sends the text (title, description, synopsis, etc.) to a translation service.
3. The translated text is stored in Tonkatsu Box's local database.
4. The user sees all content in their language, with no extra effort.

Implementation options:

Option Description Advantages Disadvantages
External translation API Use Google Translate API, DeepL API, or Microsoft Translator High quality, support for many languages Cost per use, requires API key
Local AI model Integrate a lightweight translation model (e.g., Meta's NLLB-200) Free, private, no internet dependency Higher resource consumption, variable quality
Hybrid translation Use API for major languages, local model for fallback Balance between quality and cost Implementation complexity

💡 The Little Whale's recommendation: Start with an external translation API (optional, user-provided key) and, in the long term, explore integrating a local AI model for users who prefer privacy and offline functionality.

🔄 2. Translating the User Interface to More Languages

Currently, Tonkatsu Box only has its interface in English, Russian, and Simplified Chinese. The proposal includes:

· Adding Spanish as a native interface language.
· Allowing the community to contribute translations to other languages through a collaborative system (e.g., Weblate, Crowdin).
· Using AI to assist in translating interface strings, reducing manual work.

🌍 3. Automatic Language Detection of Content

AI could automatically detect the source language of metadata and offer translation only when necessary, avoiding unnecessary translations.

🏷️ 4. Translation of Tags and Categories

Tags, genres, and categories could also be translated, allowing for more intuitive navigation in the user's language.

---

🔧 SUGGESTED IMPLEMENTATION PLAN

Phase Task Description
1 API Evaluation Research and select the most suitable translation API (Google Translate, DeepL, etc.)
2 Basic Integration Add support for translating titles and descriptions when retrieving metadata
3 Local Storage Store translations in the local database to avoid repeated API calls
4 Language Configuration Add options in Settings to choose the language of translated metadata
5 Interface Translation Add Spanish and other languages to the UI through a collaborative system
6 Optimization Implement translation caching and automatic language detection
7 Local Model (optional) Explore integrating a lightweight AI model for offline translation

---

✅ EXPECTED BENEFITS

Benefit Description
Accessibility Users from all over the world can enjoy Tonkatsu Box in their native language
Discovery Reading descriptions in your language makes discovering new content easier
Community Attracts more Spanish-speaking and other regional users
Competitiveness Differentiates Tonkatsu Box from similar applications
Privacy The option for local translation protects user data

---

🔗 REFERENCES FROM SIMILAR APPLICATIONS

Kototoro: Local Translation + OCR

Kototoro already implements an OCR + local translation system directly within its reader. Users can download translation models and use them offline. This approach demonstrates that automatic translation in content management applications is viable and valued by users.

Komi Store: Multilingual Localization

Komi Store (now Komi Store) has implemented a localization system that allows users to change the interface language and see application descriptions in their native language. Although it doesn't use AI for automatic translations, its focus on language accessibility is a model to follow.

### Describe your suggested feature



Date: 2026-03-16
Author: Community Contributor

Overview

Anizen Preview, as a fork of Tachiyomi/Mihon with enhanced downloader capabilities, can benefit from automatically updated trackers and a smart profile switcher to improve torrent download speeds while avoiding network saturation.

This proposal combines:

· An updater that fetches fresh tracker lists from reliable public sources.
· A profile system (Max, Balanced, Min, Custom) that lets users choose the number/type of trackers.
· Intelligent auto‑selection based on device capabilities (CPU/RAM/network) and tracker health.

---

Key Features

1. Tracker Updater (tracker-updater)

· Sources (verified, updated daily):
  · ngosang/trackerslist – stable, ~93 working trackers
  · XIU2/TrackersListCollection – ~143 trackers
  · newtrackon.com – top 50 with >95% uptime
· Format support: plain text, base64, lists.
· Deduplication & filtering: removes invalid/duplicate entries.
· Configurable limit: up to 500 trackers (hard limit to avoid overload).
· Scheduled updates: daily/weekly via WorkManager, plus manual refresh.

2. Profile Switcher (tracker-switcher)

· Predefined profiles:
  · Max 🌐 – up to 500 trackers (use with caution, high‑end devices only).
  · Balanced ⚖️ – intelligent selection based on device resources (default).
  · Min 🕊️ – 10‑15 highly reliable trackers (low‑bandwidth / battery saving).
  · Custom ✨ – user‑defined list.
· Manual override: switch profiles at any time from the UI.
· Auto‑profile: Anizen can automatically select a profile based on torrent category (e.g., “anime” → Balanced) or file size.

3. Intelligent Selection (Avoids Saturation)

· Health check: tests trackers with a short timeout (UDP ping / HTTP HEAD) – discards dead ones.
· Protocol prioritisation: UDP > HTTPS > HTTP (lower overhead).
· Domain grouping: limits the number of trackers from the same domain to prevent hammering a single server.
· Dynamic sizing:
  · High‑end device (≥8 cores, ≥6GB RAM) → up to 50 trackers.
  · Mid‑range → up to 30.
  · Low‑end → up to 15.
· Rotation: every 30 minutes, a percentage of trackers is swapped to distribute load.

4. Integration with Anizen Preview

· Settings UI: add a “Tracker Manager” section with profile selector, manual update button, and current tracker list viewer.
· Client‑side hook: after updating, the new tracker list is applied to all active torrents via the torrent client’s API (Transmission RPC / qBittorrent).
· Configuration file: trackers.yaml or JSON to store profiles, sources, limits, and update schedule.

---

Technical Implementation (Kotlin)

TrackerUpdater.kt

```kotlin
// Uses OkHttp and Coroutines
class TrackerUpdater(private val context: Context) {
    private val sources = listOf(
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ngosang/trackerslist/master/trackers_all.txt",
        "https://cf.trackerslist.com/all.txt",
        "https://newtrackon.com/api/stable"
    )

    suspend fun update(profile: TrackerProfile) {
        val all = mutableSetOf<String>()
        sources.forEach { url ->
            try {
                val response = httpClient.get(url).body<String>()
                all.addAll(response.lineSequence()
                    .filter { it.startsWith("http") || it.startsWith("udp") }
                    .map { it.trim() })
            } catch (e: Exception) {
                Timber.e("Failed to fetch $url: ${e.message}")
            }
        }
        val unique = all.filter { it.isNotBlank() }.distinct().shuffled()
        val selected = when (profile) {
            is Profile.Max -> unique.take(profile.limit)
            is Profile.Balanced -> selectIntelligent(unique, deviceCapabilities())
            is Profile.Min -> unique.filter { it in trustedTrackers }.take(15)
            is Profile.Custom -> profile.trackers
        }
        saveTrackers(selected)
        applyToActiveTorrents(selected)
    }

    private fun selectIntelligent(all: List<String>, caps: Capabilities): List<String> {
        val max = when {
            caps.isHighEnd -> 50
            caps.isMidRange -> 30
            else -> 15
        }
        // Prioritise UDP, group by domain
        val grouped = all.groupBy { extractDomain(it) }
        val prioritized = grouped.flatMap { (_, list) ->
            list.sortedByDescending { it.startsWith("udp") }
        }.distinct()
        return prioritized.take(max)
    }

    private fun extractDomain(tracker: String) =
        tracker.substringAfter("://").substringBefore(":").substringBefore("/")
}
```

Tu sugerencia #8 (biblioteca offline con prefetch inteligente) tiene una parte que se puede medir y otra que no. Implementé la parte medible en cero-X y estos son los números reales, por si sirven:

**Prefetch adaptado a la red**, no fijo: 3 páginas por delante en wifi, **1** con datos medidos, **0** sin red. Descargar un capítulo entero por delante gasta la tarifa del usuario sin pedirle permiso.

**El fallo que encontré probándolo con 20 cambios de capítulo seguidos**: la cancelación de un prefetch no detiene la carga en vuelo, solo la marca. Llegaron a haber **7 descargas simultáneas** de capítulos ya cerrados compitiendo con la que el usuario estaba mirando. Con un turno explícito y una espera acotada, el pico bajó a **1**.

**Caché con tope en bytes, no en páginas.** Un caché «de 20 páginas» no significa nada: 20 páginas de webtoon a 1080 px son 8 MB, y 20 de manga a doble página en un tablet de 2560 px son 160 MB.

Y el número que sí importa: con un patrón de lectura real (avanzar y rebobinar cada 20 páginas), el hit rate fue **94,4 %**. Sin rebobinado baja mucho — el prefetch solo ayuda si el usuario relee, y eso no es cierto para todos.

Tu sugerencia #2 (diagnóstico de la app con IA) — la implementé en cero-X, pero **no con IA**, y creo que es lo importante del comentario.

Lo hice con **comprobaciones deterministas** que fallan en `gradle test`:

- Un guardián que lee el manifiesto de modelos y los assets reales del APK y cruza eso contra lo que declaran los módulos. Encontró 3 módulos anunciando modelos que no existían en el APK.
- Un cazador de placeholders que busca la combinación «comentario de relleno + devolución de éxito». Encontró **14 métodos** que decían haber hecho algo sin hacerlo — incluido un `translate()` que devolvía el texto original como si fuera la traducción.

**Lo que aprendí**: el diagnóstico con IA habría sido más lento, más caro y menos fiable que siete líneas de regex bien puestas. La mayoría de los fallos de una app no son sutiles, son **mentiras escritas a mano** que nadie volvió a mirar. Para eso no hace falta un modelo: hace falta una prueba que las busque en cada compilación.

Donde sí haría falta IA es en lo que no se puede enumerar: «esta fuente se rompió y su HTML cambió de forma» no se detecta con regex. Eso sí.

Komikku es excepcional para manga, pero muchos usuarios también leen cómics occidentales (DC, Marvel, Image, etc.) que están diseñados para lectura en vista doble página. 🔧 Consideraciones Técnicas

  · Cuadrada: 0.8-1.3 (decidir por metadatos)

📐 Algoritmo de Detección Propuesto

```kotlin
fun detectPageLayout(bitmap: Bitmap, metadata: ComicMetadata): PageLayout {
    val aspectRatio = bitmap.width.toFloat() / bitmap.height.toFloat()
    
    return when {
        // Por metadatos explícitos
        metadata.format == "western" -> PageLayout.DOUBLE
        metadata.format == "manga" -> PageLayout.SINGLE
        
        // Por relación de aspecto
        aspectRatio < 0.8 -> PageLayout.SINGLE    // Vertical típico manga
        aspectRatio > 1.3 -> PageLayout.DOUBLE    // Horizontal típico cómic
        aspectRatio > 2.5 -> PageLayout.SPREAD    // Doble página completa
        
        // Por contenido (análisis simple)
        else -> detectByImageFeatures(bitmap) // Bordes, simetría, etc.
    }
}
```


Tu issue pide un ranking configurable para las fuentes del feed. Implementado en cero-X con cinco modos, y el resultado de probarlos:

| ranking | para qué sirve de verdad |
|---|---|
| **Prioridad** | el orden que puso el usuario. Manda él, y es el defecto |
| **Uso** | las que más abres primero |
| **Novedades** | las que más publican. Evita perfiles que salen vacíos |
| **Recientes** | las últimas añadidas. Útil la primera semana |
| **Alfabético** | predecible y fácil de recorrer con la vista |

Dos cosas que aprendí al probarlo:

**El alfabético tiene una trampa**: una fuente sin título desaparece si no se maneja el caso nulo. Perder entradas al ordenar es peor que ordenarlas mal, así que las que no tienen título van al final, no a la basura.

**«Por uso» y «por novedades» se pelean.** Si priorizas novedades, el feed se llena de la fuente que más publica y acabas leyendo lo que menos te interesa. Por eso el ranking tiene que ser POR PERFIL y no global: el perfil «novedades» puede ordenar por novedades mientras el perfil «lo mío» ordena por uso.
